in_text_mentions: Additionally, the histological images provided suffer from poor magnification and structural clarity, making the definitive identification of Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies highly speculative. Standard Giemsa staining typically imparts a distinct purple hue to the kinetoplast and nucleus of amastigotes (see Figure 1 example provided here); this coloration is unconvincing in Figure 2 of the published report. For a definitive diagnosis of VL/PKDL, high-magnification confirmation or molecular corroboration via nucleic acid amplification tests should have been pursued.

panels.rationale: Clear clinical photograph of a real human patient showing infiltrated hypopigmented plaques on the nape of the neck and upper back. Although the patient was initially diagnosed with leprosy in reaction, the article title ('Postkala-Azar Dermal and Visceral Leishmaniasis in a Patient from Bangladesh') establishes that these hypopigmented lesions represent post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), a well-recognized cutaneous manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar). The hypopigmented macules/patches match the vocabulary finding visceral_leishmaniasis_pkdl_hypopigmented_macules and constitute a classic PKDL presentation. The patient is stated to be a 35-year-old Bangladeshi man (adult); skin tone is judged directly from the visible, adequately lit skin as medium (Fitzpatrick III-IV). The image is clear and substantial, with no third-party copyright indication; the small corner logo is a publisher watermark, not a clinical annotation. [raw subtype: post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL)]

panels.rationale: Single whole-body 18F-FDG PET (MIP) from the article 'Visceral Leishmaniasis Mimicking Aggressive Lymphoma'. It is a real patient radiology image (prior triage: keep, not third-party) showing hypermetabolic splenomegaly and hepatomegaly with diffuse osteomedullary hypermetabolism. Disease attribution to visceral_leishmaniasis is supported by the disease-focused article title plus the captioned splenomegaly/hepatomegaly in a VL patient, satisfying the panel-specific-evidence rule; splenomegaly is the hallmark VL manifestation. The FDG-PET pattern mimicking lymphoma is a less common/recognized presentation rather than the textbook ultrasound picture, so typicality is variant. No skin, nails, lips or oral mucosa are assessable on a PET MIP, so skin_tone is null; no ethnicity or age is stated. Hepatomegaly and diffuse osteomedullary hypermetabolism are clearly present but absent from the vocabulary, so they are listed as proposed findings.

panels.figure_caption: 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT scan shows hypermetabolic splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. Small axillary lymphadenopathies appear reactive. Additionally, diffuse osteomedullary hypermetabolism is noted.
in_text_mentions: lic splenomegaly (SUVmax 14.7), homogeneous hepatic and diffuse bone marrow hypermetabolism, as well as sub-centimetric hypermetabolic right axillary lymph nodes, mildly hypermetabolic cervical and right subpectoral lymph nodes, and bilateral nonspecific tonsillar hypermetabolism (Figure 1). A bone marrow biopsy was performed and showed normal findings, while a liver biopsy revealed Kupffer cell hyperplasia and some evidence of phagocytosis without evidence of lymphoma. The absence of monoclonal lymphocytes was also confirmed by flow cytometry on both peripheral blood and bone marrow aspirate.
